extracted.intended_audience: readers of a general-interest popular science magazine (educated public; physicians and naturalists among readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles embedded in Popular Science Monthly articles on topics including mortality tables, dietary use of milk, and experimental study of ant intelligence. Targets the production and assessment of clear, evidence-based popular-science writing and domain-specific practice (actuarial tables, nutrition advice, ethology experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortality-table data completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortality tables require reliable statistics including both births and deaths and the ages of those who died.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes many English registers recorded only births or baptisms and government mortality bills often showed deaths without ages; Breslau's exact register (1687–1691) was valuable because it recorded both births and deaths with ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient sample size for mortality estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortality deductions based on small numbers are less reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley worked from only 6,193 births and 5,869 deaths yet produced useful results; the Carlisle table cautions that very young and very old ages had too few observations to be reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness of the observed population
rubrics_metrics.description: The population used to construct a table must be representative of the population to which the table will be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: London mortality bills were unsuited to represent English conditions because London's large and fluctuating population with social extremes did not reflect the whole country; Simpson deemed the Breslau table not applicable to English conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish births from christenings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate recorded christenings with actual births when constructing mortality statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Price overlooked that births and christenings were not identical (many Baptists repudiated infant baptism), leading to an incorrectly high death-to-birth ratio in the Northampton table and large government losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer whole-population enumeration when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerations of the whole population improve the ability to compare births, deaths, and population at risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlisle's advantage was that the town had enumerations allowing the determination of births and deaths in proportion to the living, improving table quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use long observation periods for table construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortality tables should be based on sufficiently long periods of observation to smooth fluctuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Price's Northampton table was based on thirty years' observations; Simpson and others used multi-year series to improve reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select conservative (higher-mortality) tables for reserves
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing among candidate tables for setting reserves/premiums, selecting the table showing higher mortality is a cautious practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Equitable Society selected the Northampton table from among new tables because it showed the highest rate of mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base reserves and premiums consistently on chosen table
rubrics_metrics.description: Actuarial reserves and premium calculations should be grounded on the mortality table chosen for the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Equitable based reserves on the Northampton table, surplus accumulated and premiums were reduced; later adoption of Carlisle again lowered premiums—illustrating the financial effects of the chosen table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust tables for local conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortality tables must be adjusted or chosen with attention to local or national conditions rather than blindly adopting foreign or urban data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simpson considered Breslau not applicable to English conditions; Dr. Price collected data from multiple English towns to obtain trustworthy tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits at extreme ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Very young and very old ages often have too few observations and should be treated cautiously in tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Carlisle table was excellent except for the very young and old ages where numbers were too few to be reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure scientific reasoning with available data
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with limited data, apply strict scientific reasoning and state limits of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley's reasoning and conclusions were 'strictly scientific' despite limited data; the text commends reasoning even when data are imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid speculative insurance practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance schemes should be founded on scientific principles rather than conjecture or gambling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts tontines and early annuities (speculative) with later scientifically-based life insurance; benevolent societies are poor substitutes for companies founded on scientific actuarial principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household milk-supply minimum
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a minimum adequate milk supply for household nutrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a household of ten persons (adults and children), five quarts per diem is stated as the least that should be consumed; children of any age may very well take a quart a day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer fresh good milk over condensed/Swiss milk
rubrics_metrics.description: Fresh milk has superior nutritive value compared with condensed (Swiss) milk and should be used when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condensed milk may be acceptable at sea or when fresh milk is doubtful, but it is unwise to use it when fresh milk is procurable; some infants will only take condensed milk, but it should be discarded as soon as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adequate quality and quantity of milk in children's diet
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should receive sufficient, good-quality milk; skimmed or watered milk is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many children get very inadequate quantities and poor quality (skimmed or watered); inadequate milk contributes to rickets and poor health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of milk consumption for digestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Milk should be taken slowly in small mouthfuls at short intervals rather than in copious draughts or after other food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infant feeding demonstrates physiological ingestion: small, gradual mouthfuls present milk to gastric surfaces to reduce to curd; adults should mimic this to avoid burdening the stomach; the better the milk quality the more severe discomfort if taken wrongly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use milk liberally in puddings and farinaceous foods
rubrics_metrics.description: Milky puddings and cereal dishes require abundance of new milk (and cream) to be palatable and nutritious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stinted or skimmed milk in rice, tapioca, and sago creates distaste; Scottish households use abundant milk and cream and a distinct pudding plate for this course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buttermilk as wholesome rural food
rubrics_metrics.description: Buttermilk should be used and proves wholesome and nutritious, especially for country and peasantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many rural districts swine may be better supplied than the peasantry; buttermilk is recommended as a nutritive, affordable option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor milk use for aged and invalids
rubrics_metrics.description: Use milk-based preparations suited to weak digestion and edentulous conditions of the aged and invalids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custard (milk and eggs) is valuable; some invalids take cold custard when hot is intolerable; rum in milk can induce intake for some invalids but should be used only under medical advice to avoid dram-drinking; for weak children, good cream diluted with two or three parts water may be substituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple aids to improve milk digestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ small remedies to make milk more digestible for those who find it disagrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add a little carbonate of soda or lime-water; eat a dry biscuit and sip the milk between mouthfuls; these measures often help digestion of milk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household prioritization of cream versus alcohol
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize nutritious cream/milk in household consumption over discretionary alcohol that provides no nutritional value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes stingy cream consumption contrasted with free use of bad sherry or claret; insufficient milk/cream contributes to nutritional loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: National agricultural policy to increase milk supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase grazing-stocks and domestic milk production to meet national milk needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author urges a large increase in grazing stocks to supply sufficient milk for the country, noting imports (America, Canada, India) can meet deficiencies but domestic production should be rebuilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing of insect senses separately
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying insect intelligence, test sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch independently with controlled experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lubbock's experiments used colored glass to test light preferences (showing graded responses), sound tests showed no effect, and smell/trail experiments (Huber) showed scent-tracking—each sense requires separate experimental attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for species variation in ethological claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not generalize across ant species without checking species-specific behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some species (e.g., genus Atta) are reported as fond of light while others avoid it; the text suggests testing differing species for opposite preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design directional-sense experiments with controlled displacements
rubrics_metrics.description: Test an ant's sense of direction by manipulating the path substrate (rotating box or moving disk) and observing whether ants register lateral direction changes or maintain heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lubbock's hat-box-on-pivot experiment and moving white-paper disk demonstrated ants retain their direction (turning with the rotated box) and can be surprised when the substrate carries them beyond intended point—suggesting registration of lateral turning rather than velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use perturbation experiments to detect communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use disturbance or disabling of individuals (e.g., killing some ants) to observe transmission of alarm or avoidance behaviors among colony members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hague's experiment: disabling ants approaching a flower-vase caused approaching ants to turn and flee; after such incidents ants avoided the vase for days—evidence of communicated alarm and avoidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand detailed, cautious interpretation of behavioral observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid accepting earlier anecdotal claims without the degree of caution, detail, and systematic experimentation necessary for strong conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes earlier observers for insufficiently cautious statements; modern observers (Bates, Moggridge, Lubbock, McCook, etc.) provide controlled experiments that leave less doubt, and the paper emphasizes careful condensation and filtering of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate pheromone/trail reliance via trail obliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Show ants rely on scent-trails by experimentally obliterating tracks and observing resulting confusion in navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huber drew a finger across an ant trail to obliterate scent and observed ants become confused and run in various directions until they found the trail again—confirming scent-tracking behavior.
